summary:
Stefania Druga's talk explores building a real-time AI Co-Scientist — an AI partner that works alongside researchers during live physical experiments, analogous to pair programming copilots but for science. She begins with a live demo: a microbit board with JackDAC sensors measuring temperature, a heat pad, a microscope, and an open-source REC camera running on-device tracking models over WiFi. The AI assistant receives sensor data and images in real time, interprets ambient conditions, and can be given experiment protocols for context-aware feedback.

Motivation comes from DeepMind's AI Co-scientist paper (multi-agent Gemini 2.0 orchestration replicating a 12-year gene transfer discovery in 2 days and proposing validated liver fibrosis drug targets) and Silver & Sutton's 'Era of Experience' paper advocating continuous real-time multimodal learning over static datasets.

The system architecture is a React frontend collecting inputs (JackDAC via WebUSB API, webcams, text, voice) as web hooks, sent to a backend communicating with the Gemini API. A critical component is the unified context assembly layer, which dynamically checks which modalities are present each message and constructs context accordingly. Experiment protocols can constrain interpretations.

She shows home experiments in Tokyo: crystallization (oversaturating salt water, gradual cooling) and fermentation. Crystal growth analysis revealed an unexpected insight — formation happens in bursts once critical saturation is reached, not gradually. CSV sensor data required a separate visualization script. She also introduces an education version of the REC camera app that runs on phones with user-provided API keys.

She closes by highlighting the broader open-source lab automation ecosystem, including the Jubilee motion platform from University of Washington (open-source lab equipment, bioreactors, pipetting automation). She envisions a future where real-time experimental data informs realistic simulations (e.g., bacteria colony growth), enabling identification of optimal conditions before running physical experiments. She also announces an upcoming AI education summit.

sections.title: Live Demo: Sensors, Heat Pad, and Camera Tracking
sections.summary: Stefania opens with a live demo connecting a microscope, microbit board with JackDAC temperature sensor, and a heat pad. The AI assistant reads ambient conditions and temperature (26°C) in real time. She shows an open-source REC camera running on-device person tracking over WiFi, notes all hardware is open source, and mentions you can define experiment protocols for context-aware feedback and create custom monitoring pages.

sections.title: Why AI Co-Scientists Matter
sections.summary: Motivation: science faces data overload and complexity. AI can analyze data at scale, generate new hypotheses, identify blind spots, and parallelize hypothesis testing (e.g., testing 100 hypotheses at once). The demo system cost under $300, built in two weeks, and is fully open source.

sections.title: DeepMind AI Co-scientist Inspiration and Era of Experience
sections.summary: Inspired by DeepMind's AI Co-scientist paper using Gemini 2.0 with multi-agent orchestration (analyzing papers, ranking hypotheses, online search). Verified against prior discoveries: replicated a gene transfer mechanism that took scientists 12 years in just 2 days without training data. Also proposed new liver fibrosis drug targets validated in wet labs. Silver & Sutton's 'Era of Experience' paper motivates moving from static human data to continuous real-time multimodal learning.

sections.title: System Architecture and Context Assembly
sections.summary: Architecture: React app frontend collecting inputs (JackDAC via WebUSB API, webcams, text, voice) as web hooks, sent to a backend communicating with Gemini API. The unified context assembly layer dynamically checks which modalities are present each message and builds context accordingly. Experiment protocols constrain interpretations. This dynamic context injection based on connected sensors and experiment type is the key engineering pattern.

sections.title: Hardware Inventory and Crystallization Experiment
sections.summary: Hardware was inventoried like cooking ingredients — sensors as inputs, cameras and boards as tools — constrained by home safety, travel, and real-time measurability. Crystallization experiment: oversaturate salt water, gradual cooling induces nucleation and crystal growth. Measured dissolution rates, nucleation sites, growth rate (affected by temperature, concentration, humidity). Recorded via microscope with fan cooling, exported CSV sensor data, plotted growth rates across samples at different temperatures (fridge vs room). Fermentation also explored.

sections.title: Crystal Growth Insights, Fermentation, and Education App
sections.summary: Crystal growth data analysis revealed an unexpected insight: crystal formation happens in bursts once critical saturation is reached, not gradually. She shows a sped-up 40-minute recording showing how humidity and temperature changed. Fermentation experiment involved controlling salt/sugar amounts and temperature to measure growth rate and CO2. She introduces an education version of the REC camera app that runs on phones with user-provided API keys for users to run their own experiments, with Lab Mine code to be open-sourced later.

sections.title: Open-Source Lab Ecosystem and Future Vision
sections.summary: She highlights the broader open-source lab automation ecosystem: the Jubilee motion platform from University of Washington, open bioreactors, and a recent workshop on automating scientific experiments (droplet manipulation, liquid handling, vial mixing). She envisions future integration where real-time experimental data from cameras and sensors informs realistic simulations (e.g., bacteria colony growth), enabling identification of optimal conditions to then recreate in physical experiments. She closes by directing people to her website for projects and papers, and announces an upcoming AI education summit.
